verdict.useCase: An AI agent that posts to a LinkedIn Page or organization on behalf of a customer (needs w_organization_social, gated behind product review), plus member-level posting via open scopes

timeToCredentials.basis: Our estimate: creating a developer app with an existing LinkedIn account and Page is instant account registration. The docs describe no wait, so we allow time to set up a Page and fill in the app form.

timeToProduction.basis: One third-party developer reported a review of about two weeks, ending in a rejection. We widen the range to allow for a resubmission. Official sources state no review wait time.

humanEffortHours.basis: Our estimate: setting up the Page and app, writing a privacy policy, documenting posting behavior and data use, gathering proof of organization registration, filling in the access form, and handling a possible rejection and resubmission.

verdict.summary: Member-level posting works with open scopes right after you create an app. Posting as a Page or organization needs w_organization_social, which is gated behind a manual product review. That review likely takes weeks and requires proof of a legally registered organization.
verdict.biggestLaunchRisk: The product review for w_organization_social can be rejected on identity vetting. One developer reported a rejection because their organizational website did not prove a legally registered, active entity.

managedCovers.text: Composio's managed-auth directory lists LinkedIn as having Composio-managed OAuth. That would let you prototype without registering your own LinkedIn app.

youNeedOwnWhen.text: The sources do not say which scopes the Composio-managed LinkedIn app covers. If you need w_organization_social to post as a Page for your own customers, confirm that scope is available. Otherwise plan to register your own app and pass LinkedIn's review.

You need your own app if you want your own branding, your own Client ID and Secret, and your own LinkedIn approval status for the Page or organization posting product. LinkedIn grants product access per app.

requirements.text: A LinkedIn member account in good standing, and agreement to the LinkedIn API Terms of Use.
If building for a company, you must have full legal authority to register an app for that entity and bind it to the Terms.
A LinkedIn Page associated with the app.
A review of LinkedIn's API and data restrictions to confirm the use case is supported.
An HTTPS redirect (callback) URL added under the app's Auth tab.
Proof of a legally registered, active organization, such as an organizational website. A GitHub Pages docs site was reportedly not accepted.

A privacy policy, plus documentation of what the app posts, how often and what data it touches. The developer wrote these for the review, but the rejection did not mention them. Whether they are formally required is not confirmed.

scopesAndNuances.text: Open permissions available to all apps are r_liteprofile, r_emailaddress and w_member_social, all via 3-legged OAuth.
Almost everything beyond the open set, including company page data, typically needs LinkedIn approval. Requesting an unapproved scope gives a 403 'Not enough permissions' error.
Posting to a Page needs w_organization_social, which one developer reported is gated behind the 'Share on LinkedIn' product review.
Marketing APIs, including Community Management, require member (3-legged) authorization. 2-legged client credentials OAuth is not available for Marketing APIs.
2-legged OAuth is not available by default. A 401 'not allowed to create application tokens' error means contacting the LinkedIn Relationship Manager or Business Development team.
LinkedIn has a Self-Serve API Program with APIs available immediately on registration, and Vetted API Programs that need eligibility and additional terms.
Standard rate limits are not published. They appear per app in the Developer Portal Analytics tab after at least one call to an endpoint. A 429 is returned when limits are exceeded.
